I uncovered it, and a light breeze soon blew it into flame. Noticing this, I made a fan from branches and used it to revive the embers whenever they nearly went out. When night returned, I was pleased to discover that the fire gave light as well as warmth. I also learned that it could improve my food. Some scraps the travelers had left behind were roasted, and these tasted much better than the berries I gathered from the trees. So I tried cooking my food the same way, putting it on the glowing embers. This ruined the berries but greatly improved the nuts and roots.

“Food grew scarce, however, and I often spent an entire day searching without success for a few acorns to ease my hunger. Because of this, I decided to leave the place where I had been living and look for somewhere I could meet my few needs more easily. I deeply regretted having to leave the fire behind. I had found it by accident and did not know how to make another. I spent several hours thinking hard about this problem, but had to give up trying to solve it. Wrapping myself in my cloak, I set off through the wood toward the setting sun. I wandered for three days before finally reaching open country. Heavy snow had fallen the night before, leaving the fields entirely white. The scene was bleak, and the cold, wet substance covering the ground chilled my feet.

“It was about seven in the morning, and I desperately wanted food and shelter. At last I saw a small hut on a rise in the ground, no doubt built for a shepherd’s use. I had never seen anything like it and examined the building with great curiosity. Its door was open, so I went inside. An old man sat near a fire, preparing his breakfast over it. Hearing a noise, he turned around. When he saw me, he screamed, fled the hut, and ran across the fields at a speed his frail body hardly seemed capable of. His appearance was unlike anyone’s I had seen before, and both it and his flight surprised me somewhat. But the sight of the hut delighted me. Here the snow and rain could not reach me, and the ground was dry. At that moment it seemed as wonderful and heavenly a refuge as Pandemonium had seemed to the demons of hell after their suffering in the lake of fire.

Indeed, I had no worries about her. She was what people call a capable woman and could manage her affairs without my help. In truth, I believe she always thought of me as a lazy boy, a useless extra, good only for building castles in the air, and was rather pleased to see me go. It was a dark night when I said goodbye. Taking along as assistants the three creditors who had caused me so much trouble, I carried the balloon, its basket, and its equipment with them by an indirect route to the place where we had stored the other supplies. Everything was still untouched, and I immediately set to work.

“It was the first of April. As I have said, the night was dark, without a single visible star. Drizzling rain fell now and then, making us very uncomfortable. My main worry, though, was the balloon. Despite its protective varnish, it was becoming heavy with moisture, and the powder could also be damaged. I therefore kept my three creditors hard at work, packing ice around the middle barrel and stirring the acid in the others. They constantly bothered me with questions about what I meant to do with all this equipment, and complained bitterly about the exhausting work. They could not see, they said, what good could come from getting soaked to the skin simply to take part in such dreadful spells. I grew anxious and worked with all my strength. I honestly believe the fools thought I had made a bargain with the devil and that my present activities were thoroughly wicked. I was therefore terribly afraid they would abandon me altogether. Still, I managed to calm them by promising to pay every debt in full as soon as I finished the business at hand. Naturally, they interpreted my promises in their own way. They doubtless imagined that, whatever else happened, I would acquire a vast amount of ready cash. Provided I paid everything I owed them, with a little extra for their work, I dare say they cared very little what became of either my soul or my body.

“After about four and a half hours, I found the balloon inflated enough. I attached the basket and loaded all my tools into it. I made sure to include the condensing equipment, a plentiful supply of water, and a large store of food, such as pemmican, which packs a great deal of nourishment into a fairly small amount of space.

I come from a small land surrounded by sea and shaded by clouds. When I picture the whole globe, with its boundless ocean and unexplored continents, my homeland seems only a tiny speck in that immense whole. Yet in intellectual power it far outweighed countries with more land and more people. It is indeed the human mind alone that created everything good or great for humanity; Nature herself was only its chief servant. England, far to the north in the restless sea, now appears in my dreams as a vast ship with a full crew, mastering the winds and riding proudly over the waves. In my boyhood she was my entire universe. Standing on my native hills, I saw plains and mountains reach as far as my eyes could follow. My countrymen’s homes dotted them, and their labor had made the land fertile. To me, that spot was the very center of the earth. The rest of the world seemed like a story that neither my imagination nor my understanding would have struggled to forget.

From the beginning, my fortunes have shown how powerfully change can shape the course of a person’s life. In my case, this was almost an inheritance. Nature had showered my father with the enviable gifts of wit and imagination, then left these winds to drive his boat through life without reason to steer it or judgment to guide the voyage. He came from an obscure family, but circumstances brought him to public attention early. He soon spent the small property inherited from his father in the glittering world of fashion and luxury he had entered. During his brief, thoughtless youth, the fashionable idlers adored him. Among his greatest admirers was the young king, who escaped political intrigue and the difficult duties of ruling to find unfailing amusement and renewed spirits in my father’s company. My father could never control his impulses. They constantly led him into trouble from which only his ingenuity could rescue him. His growing mountain of gambling and business debts would have crushed anyone else, but he bore it cheerfully, with unstoppable good humor. His presence was so essential at the dinners and gatherings of the rich that they treated his failings as forgivable and welcomed him with praise that went to his head.

Popularity of this kind, like all popularity, soon fades. Meanwhile, the difficulties he faced in every direction increased at a frightening rate, far beyond his limited means of escaping them.
